source.title: The Independence Prior of SAEs Fragments Visual Concepts
source.authors: Tommaso Mencattini; Giorgos Nikolaou; Donato Crisostomi; Thomas Fel; Francesco Montagna; E. Rodolà; Francesco Locatello

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses feature fragmentation in vision SAEs and tests a spatial-prior remedy, but it does not test dictionary-size-induced splitting or track relationships between smaller- and larger-dictionary features.
record.gate_note: The paper's fragmentation construct is spatially incomplete or disconnected activation maps for concepts, not a coarse feature being replaced across dictionary sizes by related features that partition its inputs. Its own experiments compare standard SAEs with Spatial-SAE; the feature-splitting results it cites are not its own. Rows below record its directly reported results on this related construct, linked to no claim version.
record.test_reason: The paper's 'fragmentation' is spatial: a visual concept's activation map has holes, or neighbouring patches are explained by different atoms. It is not a coarse feature replaced by finer related features as the dictionary grows. Dictionary width is fixed at c=3072 in the DINOv2 experiments. The sweeps vary sparsity budget (Table 3), regularization strength, estimator, and synthetic learned-width narrowness. None tracks feature correspondences across dictionary sizes, parent/child absorption, or hierarchy. The paper cites Chanin et al. (absorption) as motivation. Its argument that the SAE objective's independence prior causes fragmentation resembles V6 in spirit, but it concerns a different construct and does not test Matryoshka SAEs.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that tokenwise SAEs implicitly impose a patch-independence prior that vision activations violate. Spatial-SAE, derived as amortized MAP inference under MF-LRH, improves concept recovery on synthetic data (96% average win rate across sparsifiers) and improves every interpretability proxy on DINOv2 activations. The cost is reconstruction loss concentrated at high spatial frequencies, which they frame as moving along the rate-distortion-polysemanticity frontier.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares standard SAEs with a two-stream Spatial-SAE using smooth/innovation fields and graph-based spectral regularization; it does not reproduce a dictionary-size feature-splitting measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome depends on sparsifier, spatial regularization strength, smooth-field estimator, and dataset. The paper reports that excessive regularization can degrade concept recovery and reconstruction.

fits_no_version.finding: On ADE20K and on COCO-Stuff transfer, Spatial-SAE improves Normalized F1, region coherence, and LLM-rated map quality and monosemanticity over tokenwise SAEs for all four sparsifiers. For TopK, Normalized F1 rises from 57.5 to 65.4.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adding a spatial Markov-field prior to the SAE objective reduces spatial fragmentation of visual concept features and improves alignment with annotated regions.

fits_no_version.finding: The baseline's R2 advantage over Spatial-SAE grows from 0.11 at low graph frequencies to 0.37 at high graph frequencies.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The reconstruction cost of a spatial prior is concentrated in high spatial frequencies.

fits_no_version.finding: Across sparsifiers and both datasets, standard SAE codes underallocate low graph frequencies and overallocate high ones relative to concept masks. Log ratios exceed 2 at the top of the spectrum. Spatial-SAE moves the spectra toward zero.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Tokenwise vision SAEs show a consistent high-frequency spectral signature of spatial fragmentation.

record.code_released: The authors state that code, datasets, and trained models will be publicly released upon publication; release URL not stated. The implementation extends https://github.com/KempnerInstitute/overcomplete.
record.problems: The paper does not directly measure dictionary-size feature splitting, cross-size feature correspondences, or whether child features partition a parent feature's inputs. Several transfer results are stated only as ranges across sparsifiers.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 2's patch-neighborhood dependence results are described qualitatively or shown graphically and do not measure feature splitting. Synthetic concept-recovery sweeps and other objective ablations were not included because they do not measure dictionary-size split behavior or cross-size feature relations.

untested.parts: No dictionary-size sweep. No tracking of coarse versus finer features, their input coverage, or their decoder-direction proximity.
No test of size-induced splitting in large language models or open SAE releases. Only a ViT-B/14 at fixed width is used.
No nested feature families, no geometric closeness of split features, and no concept hierarchy analysis.
No parent/child latent takeover measured. The sparsity sweep (Table 3) measures Normalized F1 and R2, not absorption.
No decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents, and no count of novel latents across sizes.
Changes the objective (spatial prior) and reduces spatial fragmentation. It does not measure dictionary-size feature splitting and does not test Matryoshka SAEs.

record.verdict_notes: All rows compare the study's own method (Spatial-SAE) with baselines. They are kept with versions ['none'] as context, not as evidence on any version. The word 'split' in the intro refers to a concept spread across atoms spatially, not across dictionary sizes. Rows R3 and R4 have numeric values readable in Figure 6g–h but not in the text. For example, the TopK baseline map score appears to be 5.92 against 7.05 for Spatial-SAE, but the pairings are uncertain from the extracted figure text.

versions.untested_parts: No dictionary-size sweep or tracking of coarse and finer features, their input coverage, or directional proximity.
No test of dictionary-size splitting across large models or open SAE releases.
No test of nested feature families, geometric closeness among split features, or a concept hierarchy.
No parent-child latent takeover or test of whether changing SAE size or sparsity fixes that behavior.
No decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents or accounting of novel latents across dictionary sizes.

The paper changes the objective and measures spatial concept alignment and map coherence, but does not measure dictionary-size feature splitting or whether its features partition a coarse feature's inputs. It does not test Matryoshka SAEs.
